title: Can Engineered Hardwood Floors Be Refinished? Wear Layer Rules Explained
meta: Engineered hardwood can be refinished if the wear layer is 2 mm or thicker. How to measure yours, what sanding changes, and Wills Flooring's Snohomish prices.
keywords: can engineered hardwood be refinished, engineered hardwood wear layer thickness, refinish engineered wood floors, sand engineered hardwood, engineered floor recoat, hardwood refinishing Snohomish WA

blocks.lead: Yes, if the wear layer is at least 2 mm thick. A 3 mm or thicker veneer can be fully sanded once or twice; a 2 mm veneer takes one careful sanding; anything thinner can only be screened and recoated, never sanded to bare wood.
blocks.detail: Wills Flooring refinishes engineered floors at the same published rates as solid: $3.99 per sq ft natural, $6.50 with stain, $1.99 for a screen and recoat, with a 500 sq ft minimum. We measure the wear layer before quoting.

blocks.html: Most engineered floors we see in Snohomish went in between 2000 and 2015: builder-grade planks in Clearview and Fobes Hill subdivisions, and thicker European planks in newer acreage homes. Fifteen years of mud, dogs and wood-stove heat later, the owner asks the same thing a common Reddit thread asks: is this floor refinishable, or is it a throwaway? The answer is printed nowhere on the floor, but it is easy to find if you know where to look, and it decides whether your next step costs $1.99 or $3.99 per square foot, or means a new floor.

blocks.note: A full sand removes roughly 0.5 to 1 mm of wood depending on how flat and how scratched the floor is. Deep gouges and cupping eat more of the veneer.

blocks.text: How to find your wear layer without a spec sheet

items.text: Lift a heat register in the floor and look at the cut edge of the plank. You will see the veneer as a distinct top layer over the plywood or HDF core. Hold a ruler against it.
Where the floor meets tile or carpet, the transition strip often lifts to expose an edge. Closets and under the dishwasher are other spots where an edge shows.
Deep V-grooves between boards usually mean a thin veneer that has to hide its edges. Micro-bevels or square edges are more common on 3 mm and thicker planks, though this is a clue, not a rule.

items.d: Find the box or the invoice
items.text: A leftover carton in the garage lists the wear layer in millimeters. If the house was built in the Snohomish area after 2005, the builder or the original owner may still have the flooring paperwork.
At a free estimate we check the edge with calipers, count previous sandings and test the finish for adhesion. It takes five minutes and comes with a firm written price.

a.title: Sand to bare wood when
items: Wear layer is 2 mm or thicker, confirmed
There are scratches through the finish into the wood, gray boards or pet stains
You want to change color, which needs bare wood for stain
The factory finish is worn through in traffic lanes

b.title: Recoat instead when
items: Wear layer is under 2 mm, or you do not want to spend one of your sandings
Finish is dull and micro-scratched but there is no bare wood
You are happy with the color
The floor is under 10 years old and simply looks tired

blocks.text: What changes when an engineered floor gets sanded

items.title: The bevels disappear
items.text: Sanding takes the surface flat, which removes the small V-groove between boards. Most owners like the result: it looks like a site-finished solid floor. But if you liked the plank-by-plank definition, know that it is gone for good after the first sanding and cannot be cut back in.

items.title: Texture goes with it
items.text: Wire-brushed and hand-scraped surfaces are only a fraction of a millimeter deep. A full sand levels them into a smooth face. If the texture is what sold you on the floor, a screen and recoat preserves it; a sanding does not. We tell you this before we quote, not after.

items.title: Factory finish fights the sander
items.text: Most engineered planks carry an aluminum oxide UV-cured finish that is far harder than any site-applied coat. It clogs sandpaper and takes more passes, which is also why a recoat on it needs a proper abrasion step and a bonding primer, not just a light buff and a coat.

items.title: Stain behaves differently
items.text: Sliced veneers of oak, hickory and maple stain like solid wood of the same species. Rotary-peeled veneers show a wild, wavy grain that can blotch under stain. If you are going darker on a 2 mm floor, we test a hidden spot first and often recommend natural instead.

blocks.title: A warning for DIY-minded Snohomish owners:
blocks.text: A rented drum sander removes about 1 mm on a single aggressive pass if it sits still for a moment. On a 2 mm veneer that is half your floor. Engineered floors get sanded with a multi-head or orbital machine, fine grits and no stopping. If you sand through to the core, that board cannot be fixed with anything but replacement.
When refinishing engineered is the wrong move

items.html: The core has swelled. Floors over a damp Snohomish crawlspace sometimes cup or show raised edges. Sanding flat means removing veneer from the high edges, which can leave the core exposed at every joint.
Boards are delaminating. If the veneer is lifting from the core anywhere, the glue has failed. Sanding will catch and tear those spots. Replacement is the honest answer.
Wood-stove gaps have opened wide. Dry winter air from a stove shrinks veneer and opens joints. Refinishing does not close gaps; it just makes them cleaner. Consider a humidifier first, then recoat.

The math favors new. On a 0.6 mm floor that is already worn through, a $1.99 recoat buys a couple of years. New engineered hardwood installed at $3.25 per sq ft labor plus material may be the better spend, and we will say so at the estimate.

faq.q: How many times can engineered hardwood be refinished?
faq.a: It depends on the wear layer. A 2 mm veneer can be sanded once, a 3 mm veneer once or twice, and a 4 to 6 mm veneer two or three times. Anything under 2 mm cannot be sanded to bare wood at all and should only be screened and recoated. Each full sanding removes roughly half a millimeter to a millimeter.

faq.q: How much does it cost to refinish engineered hardwood floors?
faq.a: Wills Flooring charges the same as for solid hardwood: $3.99 per sq ft for a natural sand and refinish, $6.50 with stain, and $1.99 for a screen and recoat, all with a 500 sq ft minimum. A 900 sq ft engineered floor recoated is 900 × $1.99 = $1,791; fully sanded natural it is $3,591.

faq.q: Can you screen and recoat an engineered floor with an aluminum oxide finish?
faq.a: Yes, but it needs the right prep. Aluminum oxide is very hard and new finish will not bond to it without thorough abrasion and a bonding primer designed for factory finishes. We use the Bona system for this, which is what our Bona Certified Craftsmen status covers, and we test adhesion first.

faq.q: Can I change the color of an engineered floor?
faq.a: Only by sanding to bare wood and staining, which requires a 2 mm or thicker sliced veneer. Rotary-peeled veneers often blotch under stain. If your wear layer is too thin, the alternatives are a tinted recoat for a subtle shift or replacement, and we will tell you which at the estimate.

faq.q: How do I know if my floor is engineered or solid?
faq.a: Look at a cut edge under a floor register or transition. Solid wood shows one continuous grain top to bottom. Engineered shows a thin top layer over plywood plies or a dense fiberboard core. Most floors installed in Snohomish County homes after about 2000, especially over slabs or in wide planks, are engineered.

faq.q: Will sanding remove the wire-brushed texture on my engineered floor?
faq.a: Yes. Brushing and hand-scraping are shallow, and a full sand levels them away, leaving a smooth flat surface with no bevels. If you want to keep the texture, choose a screen and recoat, which refreshes the finish without touching the wood. The two results look quite different, so decide before work starts.
